Kahn’s algorithm:
from foundations to thesis questions

An annotated reading path for deriving, testing, and defending a focused BSCS contribution to topological ordering and DAG scheduling.

Reviewed 19 October 202620 sources · 6 themes · 4 candidate directions

Reading order

  1. Foundations and baseline policies (4 sources)
  2. Dynamic ordering and graph access (7 sources)
  3. Memory-aware ordering (5 sources)
  4. Learned priorities and recent Kahn variants (2 sources)
  5. Parallel dependency release (1 sources)
  6. Workloads and fair evaluation (1 sources)
Thesis directionsProposal planSearch & coverageDownload full BibTeX ↓

Sources support a research question. They do not establish that a proposed modification is novel or faster.

Start with the right claim

Kahn’s algorithm is indegree-based source removal. A vertex becomes ready only after every incoming dependency has been removed. A FIFO queue is one ready-set policy; this is not ordinary breadth-first traversal, which discovers vertices by distance from a starting vertex.

State the model before claiming a speedup. For an explicit adjacency-list graph, the standard sequential algorithm takes O(|V|+|E|) time with constant-time queue operations. Worst-case processing of the explicit vertices and edges costs Ω(|V|+|E|); a static exact sort cannot improve that worst-case input-reading bound in this model. Preprocessed inputs, incremental updates, restricted graph families, external memory, and parallel work or span require separate assumptions and accounting.

Ordering cost and schedule quality are different outcomes. Lower peak live memory or a shorter execution makespan can justify an ordering policy even when sorting itself takes longer. Treat the directions below as hypotheses: prove validity, include preprocessing and policy overhead, compare fair baselines, and check the closest prior art before making a novelty claim.

Foundations and baseline policies

Read Kahn first. The scheduling papers then establish why changing ready-task priority is an old idea, and why any guarantee depends on the execution model.

1962
Foundation

Topological sorting of large networks

Kahn, A. B. (1962). Topological sorting of large networks. Communications of the ACM, 5(11), pp. 558–562. https://doi.org/10.1145/368996.369025

Peer reviewedDOI: 10.1145/368996.369025Guide source E01
Finding
Introduces a procedure for topologically ordering dependency networks. The modern indegree/ready-set formulation provides the eligibility invariant for the extensions in this library.
Thesis use
Define baseline pseudocode, the ready-set invariant, cycle behavior, and the precise operation your method changes.
Limits
A new application, heap, tie-break rule, or visualization is not by itself a new algorithm. Standard static traversal already has a linear worst-case bound in the explicit input model.
Version & dates
Published 1 November 1962.
Evidence checked
Publisher metadata and abstract inspected. Original 7090 implementation and original performance measurement were not independently reproduced. Modern adjacency-list interpretation is identified as standard formulation, not a transcription of the historical implementation.

Peer reviewedDOI: 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1966.tb01709.xSource record

Candidate thesis directions

Each direction pairs an implementable change with a proof obligation and an experiment. Feasibility is a scoping judgment; novelty and performance remain to be established.

DIRECTION 01

Adaptive ready-set representation with exact policy preservation

Can switching between an exact scan and an exact heap reduce total ordering cost as the ready frontier and priority-update rate change, while emitting the same sequence?

Proposed change
Keep Kahn eligibility and one fixed release-byte score with a deterministic tie-break. At decision boundaries, use a measured cost rule to choose scanning or heap selection; rebuild from the exact score vector when switching. Charge every switch, index and score update. The existing guide already implements counters, equal-consumer grouping and bounded reductions: those operations are starting baselines.
Proof obligation
Both representations must contain exactly the ready tasks and choose the same maximum score and tie-break. Prove score equality after every completion and equivalence across switches; bound rebuild work. Equal output orders must produce equal modeled workflow-memory results.
Baselines
  • Full rescoring oracle with identical scores and tie-breaking.
  • Fixed scan and fixed heap over identical incrementally maintained scores.
  • The guide’s existing counter/grouping implementations; include all preprocessing.
Measurements
  • Complete ordering time, including preprocessing, rebuilding and stale-heap work.
  • Score equality and whole-order equality; metadata visits and key updates.
  • Peak scheduler memory and switch count, separately from live workflow bytes.
Ablations
  • Switching disabled; fixed threshold versus a training-only cost fit.
  • Hysteresis disabled; score mechanism and tie-break held constant.
BSCS feasibility
Laptop-scale implementation; start with small exact differential tests, then varying frontier width and shared-file fan-out. Tiny frontiers and frequent switching may lose.
Novelty check
This is a candidate extension, not an established gap. Audit adaptive priority queues plus XLA, Dask, Qi and LATTICE at the operation level. A heap, cached score or last-use counter is already known; require a distinct switching rule or a defensible new boundary result before calling it an algorithmic contribution.

Read with: Kahn (1962) Qi et al. (2025) Liu et al. (2026) Sukhoroslov et al. (2024)

DIRECTION 02

Bounded interval repair for dependency-insertion batches

Can a precisely bounded local Kahn repair reduce update cost on overlapping edge-insertion batches compared with full recomputation and existing dynamic methods?

Proposed change
Before execution, maintain a complete order on a fixed vertex set. For a batch that violates it, form a conservative interval covering invalidating-edge endpoints, sort its induced subgraph with Kahn, and splice it back. Fall back to global recomputation when a charged work budget is exhausted. Reject cyclic batches atomically. An invalidating edge has its source at or after its destination in the old order; this includes self-loops.
Proof obligation
Every internal and boundary-crossing edge must remain forward after splicing; no vertex may be omitted or duplicated. Detect cycles created jointly by the batch. Rejection must restore a valid prior state. Prove the fallback contract and its total cost.
Baselines
  • Global Kahn after each batch and global Kahn only when invalidated.
  • Pearce–Kelly unit-change and 2010 batch algorithms.
  • Prediction-assisted methods only when the prediction model and cost can be matched.
Measurements
  • Complete update time and tail latency, including position/adjacency maintenance.
  • Edge visits, vertices moved, interval width and fallback frequency.
Ablations
  • No fallback versus a fixed budget; fit any adaptive threshold on training traces only.
  • Single interval versus safely merged intervals with boundary checks.
BSCS feasibility
Moderate BSCS scope: insertion batches only, with no concurrent execution or vertex edits. Include long-distance edges, dense graphs and batches that create a cycle only collectively.
Novelty check
Affected-region repair, batching and fallback are established. Compare exact interval rules against Pearce–Kelly and its cited predecessors, and inspect 2024–2026 incremental work. A new name for local recomputation is insufficient; proceed only after documenting a mechanism-level difference.

Read with: Kahn (1962) Pearce et al. (2006) Pearce et al. (2010) Haeupler et al. (2012) Bender et al. (2016) McCauley et al. (2024) Deng et al. (2026)

DIRECTION 03

Budgeted lookahead under an explicit shared-output memory model

Does a bounded two-step Kahn-ready choice reduce peak live bytes enough to justify its extra ordering cost over a matched one-step policy?

Proposed change
For a fixed sequential DAG, simulate at most a declared number of candidate first tasks and their legal second choices; execute only the chosen first task. Minimize the simulated peak including allocation-before-release transients. Count each shared output once until its final consumer completes. Fix the candidate filter and tie-break before evaluation.
Proof obligation
Simulation must preserve eligibility, account for every live output, and roll back all temporary state. Candidate filtering changes the search and cannot be described as exact unrestricted lookahead. Two steps do not imply global optimality or a memory-cap guarantee.
Baselines
  • FIFO/identifier Kahn and one-step greedy memory selection under identical data semantics.
  • Model-matched LATTICE ordering and relevant Fradet heuristics where reproducible.
  • Exhaustive optimum on tiny DAGs only, with a declared search/time cap.
Measurements
  • Peak live bytes, ordering time and number of simulated choices.
  • Gap to the certified tiny-instance optimum; report timeouts separately.
  • Average memory only with explicit task durations; it is a different objective.
Ablations
  • One versus two steps; candidate budget and filter.
  • Remove secondary priority while retaining the primary memory objective.
BSCS feasibility
Small experimental scope; start with DAGs of at most eight tasks for exact oracles, then held-out workflow families. Include cases where local improvement worsens a later peak.
Novelty check
Memory-aware Kahn plus critical-path priority already appears in LATTICE. Audit graph transformations, lookahead schedulers, the guide’s E13/E32 records and recent learned priorities. A bounded search alone is not new; identify a specific model, decision rule or provable property before proposing novelty.

Read with: Kahn (1962) Marchal et al. (2013) Marchal et al. (2019) Fradet et al. (2023) Fradet et al. (2025) Benoit et al. (2026) Liu et al. (2026) Sukhoroslov et al. (2024)

DIRECTION 04

Bounded aggregation of parallel indegree reductions

Can worker-local aggregation reduce synchronization cost on high-fan-in DAGs without losing or duplicating ready tasks?

Proposed change
Use a static adjacency-array DAG and a frontier/barrier traversal first. Aggregate decrements for repeated successor destinations in bounded local batches, then publish totals and enqueue a destination exactly once at its zero transition. Include aggregation-map and frontier-merge costs. Treat actual task execution as a separate experiment.
Proof obligation
Published decrements must equal processed incoming edges. Prove exactly-once eligibility, visibility of predecessor effects, barrier/termination correctness, and cyclic-residual detection. State duplicate-edge semantics. Deterministic output requires a defined merge rule and its cost. Flush every local decrement batch before frontier completion or cycle detection; for atomic subtraction, only the update whose returned old count equals its decrement enqueues the successor.
Baselines
  • Sequential adjacency-array Kahn.
  • Per-edge atomic parallel Kahn with identical frontier semantics.
  • Taskflow static DAGs only as a separate applied-runtime comparison.
Measurements
  • Traversal time, speedup versus sequential, atomic operations and queue contention.
  • Aggregation overhead, load balance and peak auxiliary memory.
Ablations
  • Aggregation off; batch size varied.
  • Partition policy varied; deterministic merging charged explicitly.
BSCS feasibility
Higher difficulty: multicore CPU only, race detection and stress tests. Chains, low fan-in and unbalanced degrees may make aggregation slower; report those regimes.
Novelty check
Atomic readiness and batching are established. Search parallel topological sorting, dependency-counter runtimes and sparse triangular-solve scheduling before claiming a new release mechanism. Taskflow end-to-end results cannot establish an indegree-only speedup; the present review does not certify aggregation novelty.

Read with: Kahn (1962) Graham (1966) Huang et al. (2022) Sukhoroslov et al. (2024)

Build a defensible proposal

Use one candidate direction to complete this plan before committing to an implementation.

  1. Define the problem and model. Specify the graph representation, permitted updates, output, workload, resource constraints, and the outcome you intend to improve.
  2. Compare the closest three papers. Record each paper’s method, assumptions, and overlap with your idea. Identify the precise operation or evidence that your study would add.
  3. State the changed operation. Write baseline and proposed pseudocode side by side. Name the ready-set rule or maintained data structure; account for preprocessing and additional storage.
  4. Set the proof obligation. Establish dependency safety, termination, cycle detection where required, and the claimed cost bound. Separate correctness from an empirical speed or memory claim.
  5. Predefine the paired experiment. Run the same graph instances, seeds, machine, and stopping rules for every method. Measure preprocessing, ordering, schedule quality, and memory separately; report variability and failed cases.
  6. Plan limits and delivery. Reserve the first two weeks for replication and novelty checks, the next four to six for implementation and ablations, and the final two to three for analysis and writing. Adjust to your school’s calendar and state what will remain untested.

Before proposing score-maintenance work, inspect the existing guide’s XLA scheduler record, Dask ordering record, and 2026 XLA indexing change. These implementation sources can rule out novelty even when a paper search does not. A useful outcome may be a well-supported boundary on when a modification helps. Keep negative results and report costs even when the preferred hypothesis is not supported.

Search & coverage

Targeted primary-source reading from 1962 through material available on 19 October 2026. The 2026 set includes published SWAT and JPDC work plus a versioned, unreviewed LATTICE preprint. This is not a complete review of the calendar year or evidence that an unlisted method does not exist.

This is a curated, non-exhaustive search reviewed on 19 October 2026. Publication status reflects the checked source record; repeat the search before submitting a proposal.

Included

  • Primary papers with verifiable metadata and an explicit connection to topological ordering, readiness, scheduling objectives or evaluation.
  • Foundational and practical baselines retained alongside 2023–2026 work. Adjacent scheduling is not presented as a historical derivation of Kahn.
  • Each paper records inspection depth. Published papers and preprints are labeled separately; alternate versions are one study.

Excluded

  • Tutorials and repositories alone are not counted as research papers; relevant implementation evidence remains linked from the existing guide.
  • Keyword matches with no useful connection to the selected mechanisms, unverifiable metadata, and duplicate manuscript versions.
  • MoSAIC (arXiv:2610.15205v1, 10 October 2026; existing guide E35) was inspected as an emerging lead but is not a core reading recommendation here: its learned-priority concept is relevant, while the training/access setup and artifact were insufficiently specified in the inspected text for reproduction. No performance claims are adopted. The existing record is retained.

Limits of this review

  • Targeted web search and backward-reference inspection, not an exhaustive systematic review or an independently duplicated screening. Searches used English technical terms.
  • Some access was limited to abstracts or selected full-text sections. Inspect complete proofs, models and current code before implementing or defending a contribution.
  • No cited experiment or artifact was rerun for this addition; reported findings are attributed to their authors. Website tests validate reading and export behavior only.
  • Publication chronology can differ from proceedings/issue citation years; affected records retain explicit notes. Preprints can change after this cutoff.
  • The four directions are our synthesis and scoping judgments. Establish the precise difference from prior art, then preregister a fair experiment; empirical improvement alone does not prove novelty.
